summary: A country spanning Europe and Asia that was once the center of the Byzantine and Ottoman empires; the republic was founded by Atatürk in 1923, and Istanbul is a famous historic and cultural city.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: The Turks converted to Islam in Central Asia in the 10th century, and after the Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantines at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 and entered Anatolia, Islam replaced Christianity as the mainstream. The Ottoman Empire governed under the Hanafi school of Sunnism, and after 1517 the sultan also served as caliph. In 1923 Atatürk founded the republic, in 1924 he abolished the caliphate and set up the Directorate of Religious Affairs to manage mosques, pursuing secularism; after the Justice and Development Party came to power in 2002, the role of religion in public life expanded again.

ranking.name: Islam (Alevi)
ranking.description: Alevism is an Islamic tradition peculiar to Anatolia that reveres Ali and follows the 13th-century mystic Haji Bektash Veli as its spiritual teacher, holding rituals in the gathering hall called the "cemevi," in which men and women take part together, accompanied by music and dance. In the 16th century the Ottoman Empire was hostile to the Shia Safavid dynasty, and the Alevis, regarded as pro-Safavid "Qizilbash," were suppressed, so believers withdrew to rural mountain areas. After the founding of the republic many Alevis supported secularism, but their places of worship have still not been formally recognized officially.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From the 1920s the Turkish Republic pursued secularism, excluding religion from law and education and so giving room for a non-religious way of life. In recent years urbanization and the spread of higher education, together with some young people's aversion to the politicization of religion, have gradually increased the number of those in large cities such as Istanbul and Izmir who regard themselves as having no religion or not believing.

ranking.name: Christianity and Judaism
ranking.description: Anatolia was the Christian heartland of the Byzantine Empire, but the Armenian genocide of 1915, the 1923 population exchange between Greece and Turkey (about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians were moved to Greece) and the 1955 anti-Greek riots in Istanbul sharply reduced the number of Christians. The Jewish community consists mostly of descendants of Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 and accepted by Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II, most of whom moved to Israel after 1948.

religion.background: Anatolia was an important region of early Christianity, and the Byzantine Empire made Constantinople the center of Orthodoxy. After the Seljuk Turks entered in the 11th century Islam gradually became the majority; in 1453 the Ottoman Empire took Constantinople and afterward governed a multi-religious empire under Sunni Islam. The wars, massacres and population exchanges of the early 20th century greatly reduced the Christian population. After the founding of the republic in 1923 secularism was pursued, and in recent years the relationship between religion and politics has again become the core of social controversy.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish belongs to the Oghuz branch of the Turkic family and entered Anatolia with the Seljuk Turks in the 11th century. The written language of the Ottoman period was mixed with a great deal of Arabic and Persian; in 1928 Atatürk carried out a script reform, replacing the Arabic alphabet with the Latin alphabet, and in 1932 the Turkish Language Association was founded to purify the language of foreign words. Through nationwide unified public education Turkish became the mother tongue of the great majority of citizens.

ranking.name: Kurdish
ranking.description: Kurdish speakers are found mainly in the southeast, mostly speaking the Kurmanji dialect, with some Zazaki. The early republic pursued a single-nation policy, and from 1983 to 1991 a law even banned the use of Kurdish in public. Armed conflict involving the Kurdistan Workers' Party from 1984 made the language issue even more sensitive, and restrictions were relaxed only in the 2000s in applying to join the European Union; in 2009 a state Kurdish-language television channel began broadcasting and schools also offered elective courses.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic speakers are mainly the Arab-descended inhabitants of the southern Hatay Province (incorporated from French Syria in 1939) and of the Mardin and Siirt area. After the outbreak of the Syrian civil war in 2011 Turkey took in more than three million Syrian refugees, making Arabic more common in southern cities such as Gaziantep and in Istanbul.

language.history: Turkish derives from the Turkic language of Central Asia and entered Anatolia with the Seljuk Turks in the 11th century. In the Ottoman period "Ottoman Turkish," blending Arabic and Persian, took shape, far removed from popular spoken usage. In 1928 Atatürk carried out a script reform, switching to the Latin alphabet and purifying foreign vocabulary, which greatly raised the literacy rate. The republic long pursued a single-language policy, and minority languages such as Kurdish were suppressed, with restrictions relaxed only gradually from the 2000s.

ranking.name: Döner kebab
ranking.description: Marinated lamb, beef or chicken is stacked on a vertical rotating spit and slowly roasted, then shaved into thin slices and put in bread or on a plate, served with salad and sauce.
ranking.history: The vertical rotating spit took shape in the 19th century in Bursa in the Ottoman Empire, and "döner" means "rotating." From the 1960s large numbers of Turkish workers went to West Germany under bilateral agreements, and in the 1970s Turkish immigrants in Berlin put the sliced meat in bread with salad and sauce, inventing today's globally popular "döner sandwich." Döner is therefore not only a Turkish dish but also one of the most popular fast foods in Germany.

ranking.name: Baklava
ranking.description: Dozens of layers of extremely thin phyllo are brushed one by one with butter, filled with crushed pistachios or walnuts and baked, then drenched in syrup when they come out of the oven, crisp, fragrant and sweet.
ranking.history: Baklava was refined in the palace kitchens of Topkapı Palace in the Ottoman Empire and became the court's representative dessert. The Ottoman period also had a tradition of the "baklava procession": on the 15th day of Ramadan each year the sultan would reward the Janissaries with trays of baklava. Gaziantep in the southeast is famous for pistachio baklava, and in 2013 "Gaziantep Baklava" became the first Turkish product to obtain EU protected geographical indication.

ranking.name: Lahmacun
ranking.description: A thin round of dough is spread with a topping of ground meat, tomato, onion, chili and herbs, baked in a very hot oven until crisp, and rolled up with lettuce and lemon juice to eat.
ranking.history: Lahmacun comes from the Arabic "lahm bi'ajin" (meat with dough) and derives from a food tradition shared by southeastern Turkey, northern Syria and the Armenians, among others. Şanlıurfa and Gaziantep in southeastern Turkey are known for the spicy version, and in the 20th century it spread across the country as southeastern migrants poured into large cities such as Istanbul. Cheap and quick, it is one of the most popular street snacks in Turkey.

ranking.name: İskender kebap
ranking.description: Slices of döner meat are laid on cut pieces of pide bread and topped with tomato sauce and sizzling browned butter, with yogurt on the side.
ranking.history: İskender kebap is named after its inventor, İskender Efendi, who, according to his family, began making kebab in Bursa in 1867 by changing from stacking the meat horizontally to grilling it vertically, then serving it with tomato sauce and butter. His descendants still run restaurants in Bursa and own the trademark. The dish is therefore closely tied to Bursa and is one of the best-known regional dishes of Turkey.

ranking.name: Turkish delight (lokum)
ranking.description: Chewy candy blocks cooked for a long time from sugar, starch and water, flavored with rose water, pistachio or hazelnut and coated all over with powdered sugar.
ranking.history: Similar sweets already existed in the Ottoman Empire, and in 1777 the confectioner Hacı Bekir from Anatolia opened a shop in Istanbul and improved the recipe with refined sugar and starch, making the candy famous; his shop is still in business today. In the 19th century a British traveler took it back to Europe and named it "Turkish Delight." In Turkey lokum is a traditional sweet for entertaining guests at festivals and for serving with Turkish coffee.
